instruction: Why is the hospital so big?
response: Great question! Children's Hospital is big because it has lots of different rooms for lots of different things. There are rooms where doctors check on kids, rooms with special machines that can take pictures of the inside of your body, rooms where families can rest, and even playrooms! It's kind of like a small city — everything kids and their families need is all in one building so nobody has to go far.

instruction: What does the B in my room number mean?
response: The letter in your room number tells you which zone of the hospital you're in! Children's Hospital is in Zone B. So if your room number starts with B, that means you're right here in the children's part. The number after the letter tells you which floor you're on. For example, B2-503 means Zone B, floor 2, room 503. It's like an address inside the hospital!

instruction: Why do hospitals smell funny?
response: You know how your family might clean the kitchen with special cleaning sprays? The hospital uses special cleaners too — really strong ones — to make sure everything is super clean and free of germs. That's the smell you notice! It might seem funny, but it actually means the hospital is doing a good job keeping everything safe and clean for you.

instruction: What is that beeping sound I keep hearing?
response: Those beeping sounds come from machines called monitors. They keep track of things like how fast your heart is beating or how much oxygen is in your blood. The beeps are like little check-ins — the machine is saying 'everything's okay!' Sometimes a beep means a nurse should come take a look, but most of the time it's totally normal. If a beep ever worries you, you can always ask your nurse about it.

instruction: Why do doctors wear those pajama-looking clothes?
response: Those comfy-looking clothes are called scrubs! Doctors and nurses wear them because they're easy to move around in and super easy to wash. Since hospitals need everything to be really clean, scrubs can be washed at very high temperatures to get rid of all the germs. Plus, they don't have buttons or zippers that could get in the way when doctors are working. Pretty smart, right?

instruction: Why do I have to wear this bracelet?
response: That bracelet on your wrist is called an armband, and it's actually really important! It has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. Before anyone gives you medicine or does a test, they scan or check your bracelet to make 100% sure they have the right person. It's like your own special hospital ID. If you have any allergies, you might get a red bracelet too, so everyone on your care team knows.

instruction: Why do people keep asking me my name and birthday?
response: I know it might feel a bit silly to keep saying it over and over! But every time someone asks your name and birthday, they're checking your armband to make sure you're getting exactly the right care. It's one of the most important safety rules in the hospital. Think of it like a secret password — it keeps you safe!

instruction: What is that thing on my finger that glows red?
response: That little clip is called a pulse oximeter, and the red glow is just a tiny light! It shines through your finger to measure how much oxygen is in your blood. It doesn't hurt at all — it's just using light to peek at what's happening inside. Pretty cool, huh? If it feels uncomfortable, let your nurse know and they can adjust it.

instruction: Why can't I bring my own balloons?
response: That's a really good question! Some balloons are made of a material called latex, and some people are very allergic to it. An allergic reaction can make someone really sick. So to keep every kid in the hospital safe, latex balloons aren't allowed. But don't worry — if someone wants to send you something fun, they can bring mylar balloons (the shiny, foil kind) or other cool gifts instead!

instruction: What is the SMILE Room?
response: The SMILE Room is one of the coolest rooms in the hospital! It's on the sixth floor in room B6-261, and it's full of awesome sensory stuff — like bubble columns that change colour, fibre optic lights you can hold, mirrors, and relaxing music. It's designed to help you relax or have fun with different sounds, lights, and textures. You can ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if you can visit it!

instruction: Who is Ollie the Clown?
response: Ollie is a really special person at Children's Hospital! Ollie is a therapeutic clown, which means Ollie is specially trained to make kids laugh, play games, and have fun while they're in the hospital. Ollie helps make hospital days feel a little more normal and a lot more silly. If you see Ollie around, get ready to smile!

instruction: What is a Child Life Specialist?
response: A Child Life Specialist is someone whose whole job is to help kids feel less scared and more comfortable in the hospital. They can explain what's going to happen before a procedure, teach you ways to feel brave, and play games with you. They're kind of like a hospital buddy who's an expert at making things less worrying. You can ask your nurse to set up a visit with one!

instruction: Why are there so many different people taking care of me?
response: Each person on your care team is an expert at something different. Your doctor figures out what's going on with your body. Your nurse takes care of you every day and checks how you're feeling. There might also be a physiotherapist who helps you move, a dietitian who makes sure you're eating the right foods, and more. They all work together like a team to take the best care of you!

instruction: What does a pharmacist do at the hospital?
response: A pharmacist is the medicine expert! They make sure that all the medicines you get are the right ones, in the right amount. The Children's Hospital has its own pharmacy right on the first floor near the B1 entrance. If you or your parents ever have questions about a medicine, the pharmacist can explain everything. Your nurse can help arrange a visit with one.

instruction: What is a volunteer?
response: Volunteers are really kind people who come to the hospital to help out, even though it's not their job. Some volunteers help families find their way around the hospital, and some help out in playrooms or bring fun activities to kids. At Children's Hospital, you can find guide volunteers near the B1 entrance and B2 lobby. They wear special badges so you can spot them!

instruction: Who is the person who comes to play music?
response: That's a music therapist! They're a real trained musician who uses music to help kids in the hospital feel better. Music therapy can help with all sorts of things, like helping you relax or just having fun. You don't need to know how to play any instrument or sing — everyone can join in. It's one of the really special things about being at Children's Hospital.

instruction: Why does the doctor have a stethoscope?
response: A stethoscope is that cool instrument that hangs around a doctor's neck! When they put the round part on your chest or back, it lets them hear your heart beating and your lungs breathing. It works kind of like super-powered ears. It might feel a little cold when they first put it on you, but it doesn't hurt at all.

instruction: What are medical students?
response: Medical students are people who are still in school learning how to be doctors. They've already finished university and now they're doing extra years of special doctor school. They might help take care of you, but there's always a fully trained doctor watching over everything they do. It's kind of like having a student driver — there's always someone experienced right there with them!

instruction: When do I get to eat?
response: At Children's Hospital, meals come at these times: breakfast is between 7:45 and 8:45 in the morning, lunch is between 11:45 and 12:45, and dinner is between 4:45 and 5:45. But here's something important — sometimes your doctor might need you to wait before eating, especially before certain tests. So always check with your nurse before munching on anything, okay?

instruction: Can I pick what I want to eat?
response: Yes, kind of! At breakfast, you'll get a form where you can pick what you'd like to eat for the next day. The choices will depend on what your doctor says is okay for you. The hospital can make lots of different kinds of food, including vegetarian and food for allergies. If you have a favourite food or something you really don't like, let your nurse know!

instruction: Is there a Tim Hortons here?
response: There's a food place called 'On the Go featuring Tim Hortons' on the second floor of Zone B in the big atrium area. It's open on weekdays from 6:30 in the morning until 8:00 at night, but it's closed on weekends and holidays. Your parent or caregiver can grab something there. There are also vending machines near the elevators on the 1st and 3rd floors of Zone B if you need a snack!

instruction: Can I use my tablet in the hospital?
response: Yes! You can bring your own tablet, phone, or device to use during your stay. The hospital even has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live TV for free or log in to your own streaming apps. If you need help with the WiFi, your parent or caregiver can call the Data Valet at 1-800-642-3958. Having your own stuff can make the hospital feel a lot more like home!

instruction: Why do I have to wash my hands so much?
response: Washing your hands is like having a superpower against germs! In a hospital, keeping hands clean is extra important because germs can spread easily and make people who are already not feeling well even sicker. You should wash your hands before eating, after using the bathroom, and whenever you enter or leave a room. The hospital has special hand sanitizer stations everywhere to make it easy.

instruction: Can I bring my stuffed animal to the hospital?
response: Absolutely! Bringing a favourite stuffed animal or comfort toy from home is a great idea. It can make your hospital room feel more cozy. Just make sure it's clean — the hospital likes toys that can be wiped down or washed easily. Try not to bring too many things though, because there isn't a huge amount of space. Your special stuffie should stay with you and not be shared with other kids, to keep everyone healthy.

instruction: Why can't I get out of bed by myself?
response: Your nurse wants to make sure you don't slip or fall, especially if you're feeling a little wobbly from being in bed or from medicine. The floors can be slippery sometimes too. Before you get up, just press your call button or ask a grown-up to let your nurse know. They might ask you to wear special non-slip socks to help keep you safe. It's all about keeping you from getting a boo-boo!

instruction: What is the call button for?
response: The call button is like a magic button that lets your nurse know you need something! It's usually near your bed. When you press it, a light goes on at the nurses' station and they come to check on you. You can press it anytime — if you're thirsty, if something hurts, if you need to go to the bathroom, or even if you just have a question. That's what it's there for!

instruction: What is an IV?
response: An IV stands for 'intravenous,' which is a big word that means 'into a vein.' It's a tiny, thin tube that goes into a small vein, usually in your hand or arm. Through that tube, doctors can give you medicine or fluids your body needs without you having to swallow anything. Getting the IV put in might pinch for a second, but after that it usually doesn't hurt. If it ever bothers you, tell your nurse right away!

instruction: What does an X-ray machine do?
response: An X-ray machine takes pictures of the inside of your body — kind of like a camera, but instead of seeing your face, it can see your bones! It uses a special kind of light that you can't see or feel. You just have to hold very still for a few seconds while it takes the picture. It doesn't hurt at all. The picture helps your doctor see if anything inside needs attention.

instruction: Why does the blood pressure cuff squeeze my arm?
response: That squeezy thing is a blood pressure cuff! It puffs up like a balloon around your arm to check how hard your heart is pumping blood through your body. It squeezes for just a little bit and then lets go. It might feel tight and funny, but it's totally safe and it's over really quick. Think of it as your arm getting a quick hug!

instruction: What are those sticky things on my chest?
response: Those are called electrodes, and they're stuck on with little sticky pads. They're connected to a heart monitor, which is a machine that watches your heartbeat and shows it as a wiggly line on a screen. They don't hurt — they just sit there and listen to your heart doing its thing! When it's time to take them off, it's kind of like pulling off a bandage.

instruction: What is a thermometer doing in my ear?
response: An ear thermometer is a quick way to check your temperature — that means how warm your body is. It works by reading the heat coming from inside your ear. It only takes a second and it doesn't hurt! It might feel a little tickly. Your nurse checks your temperature to make sure your body is doing okay.

instruction: Why does the nurse wear gloves?
response: Nurses wear gloves to protect both you and themselves from germs. The gloves are a barrier, kind of like a shield, that keeps germs from passing back and forth. They put on fresh, clean gloves before they help each patient, and throw them away when they're done. It's one of the many ways the hospital keeps everyone safe and healthy!

instruction: What is that pole with the bag hanging on it?
response: That's called an IV pole! The bag hanging on it is filled with special fluid or medicine that drips slowly through a tube and into your IV. The pole has wheels on the bottom so you can roll it along with you if you need to get up and walk around. Some kids even give their IV pole a name — you can too if you want!

instruction: Is there a playroom I can go to?
response: Yes! Children's Hospital has some awesome spaces for playing. There's Ashley's Backyard in room B6-259 — it's a nature-themed playroom for younger kids and their families. There's also the School-Age Activity Room in B6-065 where you can do crafts, play board games, work on puzzles, and build with LEGO. Child Life staff and volunteers set up fun activities there too. Ask your nurse if you're allowed to visit!

instruction: What are Bravery Beads?
response: Bravery Beads are really special! They're beads you collect to make a necklace or string that tells your personal hospital story. Each bead stands for something you went through — like getting an IV, having a test done, or being really brave during a procedure. Over time, you build up this amazing collection that shows everything you've been through. It's your very own bravery necklace!

instruction: Can I do art while I'm here?
response: Yes! Children's Hospital has an Art Therapy program. An art therapist can help you draw, paint, or create things as a way to express how you're feeling. You don't have to be a great artist — it's all about having fun and getting your feelings out. It can be really relaxing too. Ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist about it!

instruction: Are there dogs in the hospital?
response: Sometimes, yes! Children's Hospital works with a group called St. John Ambulance to have therapy dogs visit patients. These dogs are specially trained to be gentle and calm, and petting them can make you feel really happy and relaxed. Ask your care team if there's a therapy dog visit coming up — they can let you know! Regular pet visits from home aren't usually allowed, but there can be special exceptions.

instruction: What is the Heroes' Circle?
response: The Heroes' Circle is a super cool program where kids learn breathing exercises, relaxation techniques, and even some martial arts moves! They visit kids in the hospital every week, both in patient rooms and in the clinic. It's a fun way to feel strong and learn tricks that can help you feel calmer. You can ask your nurse about it or email info@kidskickingcancer.ca to learn more.

instruction: Can I watch TV in my room?
response: Yes you can! The hospital has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free. If you have a streaming account like Netflix or Disney+, you can log in and watch your own shows too. There's free WiFi available, and your parent or caregiver can call 1-800-642-3958 if you need help connecting.

instruction: Can I make phone calls?
response: Yep! There are patient telephones you can use for local and toll-free calls for free. You can also use your own cell phone to call or text your family and friends. Staying connected to people you love is important, and the hospital wants to make that easy for you.

instruction: Why do the doors lock at night?
response: Some doors in the hospital lock at certain times to help keep everyone safe, especially at night when it's quieter. The main entrance to the B Tower is open from 6:00 in the morning until 8:30 at night. After that, security guards are at the doors to make sure only the right people come in. It's like how you lock your front door at home — it helps everyone inside feel safe and protected.

instruction: Who are the security guards?
response: Security guards are like the hospital's safety helpers. They walk around the building to make sure everyone is safe. They can also walk you or your family to your car if it's dark outside — all you have to do is call them! They're not scary at all. They're here to help protect patients, families, and everyone who works at the hospital.

instruction: Why can't people visit if they're sick?
response: When someone has a cold or a tummy bug, they carry germs that could spread to kids in the hospital. Since many kids here are already not feeling well, catching extra germs could make them feel a whole lot worse. That's why the hospital asks people who are feeling sick to wait until they're better before visiting. It's a way of being a really good friend — protecting others by staying home until you're well!

instruction: What is that sign on the door of some rooms?
response: Sometimes a room has a special sign because the patient inside needs extra protection from germs, or because they have germs that shouldn't spread to others. The sign tells visitors to check with the nurses before going in. You might need to wear gloves, a gown, or a mask before entering. It's not scary — it's just another way the hospital keeps everyone safe!

instruction: Why can't I bring flowers to someone?
response: Some parts of the hospital don't allow flowers because certain plants can carry germs or cause allergies for patients who are very sensitive. There's also a plant called a poinsettia that's never allowed because it contains stuff similar to latex, which some people are really allergic to. If you want to cheer someone up, cards, drawings, or mylar balloons are great alternatives!

instruction: Why does everything need to be so clean?
response: When you're at home, a few germs are no big deal because your body is strong enough to fight them off. But in a hospital, many kids are already using their body's energy to get better, so they can't fight off extra germs as easily. That's why the hospital cleans everything so carefully and asks everyone to wash their hands a lot — it gives every kid the best chance of getting better faster!

instruction: Can my mom or dad sleep here with me?
response: Yes! Most patient rooms at Children's Hospital have a spot where a parent or caregiver can sleep right near you. There are usually sleeper chairs or fold-out beds. Your parent will need their own pillow and can get clean sheets and blankets from the nurses. You won't have to be alone at night if you don't want to be. Just remember — you need to sleep in your own hospital bed so the nurses can check on you easily.

instruction: Can my friend come visit me?
response: Friends can visit! But there are a few things to know. The hospital asks visitors to check with the nurses on your unit first to find out the best times for visiting. For inpatients, up to two care partners can be at your bedside at one time. Your friend should wash their hands when they come in and when they leave, and they shouldn't visit if they're feeling sick. But if everyone's healthy, visitors are welcome!

instruction: Can my brother or sister visit me?
response: Usually yes! Siblings can visit, but just like all visitors, they should wash their hands and shouldn't come if they're feeling sick. The hospital also asks visitors to check with the nurses first about the best times. Having your brother or sister visit can really cheer you up! The hospital also has some fun programs that siblings can be part of, like the Heroes' Circle.

instruction: What is the Ronald McDonald House?
response: Ronald McDonald House is a special home away from home for families who have a child in the hospital. If your family lives far from London, they can stay there instead of a hotel. It's close to the hospital so they can visit you easily. It has bedrooms, a kitchen, and common areas where families can relax. Your care team can help your family find out if they can stay there.

instruction: What is the family lounge?
response: The family lounge is called the Culliton Family Lounge, and it's in room B6-110. It's a comfy space where you and your family or friends can hang out together and relax away from your hospital room. Sometimes the hospital holds special group events and family coffee hours there too. It's a nice place to take a little break!

instruction: Why do I have to take medicine if I feel fine?
response: That's such a smart question! Sometimes medicine works quietly in the background to help your body keep getting better, even if you already feel okay. It's kind of like wearing a seatbelt in a car — you might feel fine, but it's still protecting you. Your doctor and nurse know exactly why you need each medicine, so if you're curious, you can ask them to explain!

instruction: Why does the nurse check on me at night?
response: Even when you're sleeping, your nurse peeks in to make sure you're comfortable and safe. They might quickly check your temperature or listen to how you're breathing. They try to be super quiet so they don't wake you up! It's actually a really nice thing — even in the middle of the night, someone is watching out for you.

instruction: Why does blood need to be tested?
response: Your blood carries lots of important information about how your body is doing. When the doctor takes a little bit of blood to test, they're looking at things like how many red and white blood cells you have and how your body is working on the inside. It helps them understand the best way to help you feel better. The test itself is quick — just a small poke!

instruction: What does an ultrasound do?
response: An ultrasound uses sound waves — kind of like the echos a dolphin makes — to create pictures of what's inside your body. A person puts some cold, squishy gel on your skin and then moves a little wand-like tool over it. The sound waves bounce back and make a picture on a screen. It doesn't hurt at all! The gel might just feel a little gooey and cold.

instruction: Why do I need to tell the nurse when I go to the bathroom?
response: Sometimes the doctors need to keep track of how your body is working, and going to the bathroom is one of the clues! It helps them know if you're drinking enough water and if your body is doing its job properly. It might feel a little weird to talk about, but it's totally normal in a hospital. Your nurse has heard it all before, so don't be shy!

instruction: What does 'nil by mouth' mean?
response: 'Nil by mouth' is a way of saying you can't eat or drink anything for a while. It usually happens before a test or procedure where your tummy needs to be empty. I know that can be tough, especially if you're hungry! But it's really important for keeping you safe. Your nurse will let you know when you can eat and drink again.

instruction: How do I find my way around this place?
response: The hospital has lots of helpers for that! You can find information desks that are open Monday to Friday from 8 in the morning to 8 at night, and there are friendly guide volunteers near the B1 entrance and B2 lobby. There's also an app called MazeMap that has a map of the whole hospital — your parent can download it on their phone. And there are QR codes you can scan near the elevators to pull up a map too!

instruction: Where is the hospital?
response: Children's Hospital is at 800 Commissioners Road East in London, Ontario. It's part of a bigger place called the Victoria Hospital site, and the children's part is in an area called Zone B. If your family is driving here, the closest parking is Parking Lot 8, which is a parking garage you can get to from Baseline Road.

instruction: What floor am I on?
response: You can figure that out from your room number! The second number in your room tells you the floor. For example, if your room is B6-something, you're on the 6th floor of Zone B. If it's B2-something, you're on the 2nd floor. Pretty simple once you know the trick! And if you ever get turned around, any staff member can help you find your way.

instruction: Why are hospital beds so different from my bed at home?
response: Hospital beds are specially designed to help take care of you! They can be raised and lowered, the head part can tilt up so you can sit and eat or watch a show, and they have rails on the sides to keep you from rolling out. Some even have buttons you can push yourself! They might not be as cozy as your bed at home, but they're built to make your care easier.

instruction: Do doctors and nurses live at the hospital?
response: Ha, it can seem like that sometimes! But no, doctors and nurses go home to their own families just like your family comes to visit you. They work in shifts — that means one group works during the day and another group takes over at night. That's why you might see different nurses at different times. But someone is always here to take care of you, 24 hours a day!

instruction: Why do nurses change shifts?
response: Taking care of patients is really important work, and it takes a lot of energy! To make sure your nurses are at their best and not too tired, they take turns in shifts. When one nurse finishes their shift, they tell the next nurse all about you and how you're doing — this is called a shift change report. Your family is even invited to listen in and ask questions!

instruction: What is a gown and why do I have to wear one?
response: A hospital gown is that loose, open-backed shirt you wear. You don't always have to wear one — many kids can wear their own comfy clothes! But sometimes doctors need to be able to check on your body easily, or you might have tubes or wires that need to go through the gown. Ask your nurse whether you can wear your own PJs — they'll let you know!

instruction: Why is the hospital open all day and all night?
response: People can feel sick or get hurt at any time — in the morning, at lunchtime, or even in the middle of the night. That's why the hospital never closes! There are always doctors, nurses, and other helpers here, no matter what time it is. Even when you're sleeping, there are people watching over you and all the other kids in the hospital.

instruction: What is a wheelchair for?
response: A wheelchair helps people get around when they can't walk easily — maybe because they're tired, hurt their leg, or just had a procedure. The hospital has wheelchairs you can borrow, usually near the entrances. If you can't find one, just ask a staff member or volunteer and they'll help. Some kids even think it's fun to zoom around in one!

instruction: What's that thing they clip on my arm that puffs up?
response: That's a blood pressure cuff! It wraps around your arm and puffs up with air to measure your blood pressure, which tells the nurse how well your heart is pumping blood around your body. It squeezes for a few seconds and then slowly lets go. It feels funny and tight, but it's totally harmless and over really quickly!

instruction: What is that clear liquid in the IV bag?
response: Most of the time, that clear liquid is a special fluid that helps keep your body hydrated — kind of like drinking water, but it goes straight to where your body needs it most. Sometimes medicine is mixed in too. Your nurse can tell you exactly what's in your bag if you're curious! It drips in slowly so your body can handle it well.

instruction: Why is there a sink in every room?
response: Having a sink in every room makes it super easy for everyone to wash their hands. Remember, hand washing is the number one way to stop germs from spreading in a hospital! Nurses wash their hands before and after they help you, visitors should wash when they come in and leave, and you should wash yours too, especially before eating. That little sink does a really big job!

instruction: Can I go outside while I'm in the hospital?
response: That depends on what your doctor says. Some kids can go to special areas like Alex's Butterfly Garden, which is a beautiful, peaceful outdoor garden in the hospital's D Zone on level 2. It has benches and a water fountain. But you'll need to check with your nurse first to make sure it's okay. If you can't go outside, there are still lots of fun indoor spaces to explore!

instruction: What happens if there's a fire in the hospital?
response: The hospital has a really good plan for emergencies like that! There are fire alarms, sprinklers, and fire doors throughout the building, and all the staff practice what to do so they can keep everyone safe. The most important thing is to listen to your nurse — they'll tell you exactly what to do. The hospital is built with lots of safety features, so you're in very good hands.

instruction: Why does my room have a curtain?
response: The curtain is there to give you privacy! If you're sharing a room with another patient, or when a nurse needs to check on you, the curtain can be pulled closed so you have your own private space. It's like a soft, movable wall. If you ever want your curtain open or closed, just ask!

instruction: What is the Paediatric Family Resource Centre?
response: The Paediatric Family Resource Centre is a special room on the 1st floor of Zone B, room B1-006. It's a quiet place where your parents can find information about your health, get help filling out forms, and talk to people who have been through similar experiences. It's open most days of the week. Your family can pop in anytime during its open hours!

instruction: Why do some kids get to wear their own clothes?
response: Wearing your own comfy clothes from home can make you feel more like yourself! The hospital encourages kids to wear their own PJs, slippers, and clothes when it's possible. Sometimes you might need a hospital gown instead, like if you're going for a test or if there are tubes that need easy access. But most of the time, your own clothes are totally fine — bring your favourites!

instruction: What is the Sanctuary?
response: The Sanctuary is a very quiet, peaceful room in Zone C, level 3, room C3-402. It's open all day and all night for anyone who wants some quiet time, whether for praying, thinking, or just being calm. All patients and families are welcome there, no matter what they believe. It's a really nice place to go when you want a moment of peace.

instruction: What does the hospital do at night?
response: The hospital doesn't go to sleep — there are always people here working! Nurses check on patients, doctors are available if anything urgent comes up, and security guards walk around to keep everyone safe. The lights get dimmer and things get quieter, but there's always a team of people looking after you. You can rest easy knowing that!

instruction: What is that thing that squeezes my finger?
response: That clip on your finger is called a pulse oximeter. It uses a little red light to see how much oxygen your blood is carrying. Oxygen is what you breathe in, and your blood carries it all around your body. The clip just checks that everything is moving along the way it should. It doesn't hurt — it just clips on gently and does its thing!

instruction: What happens to the garbage in a hospital?
response: The hospital is really careful about garbage! Some garbage, like used bandages or gloves, goes into special bins because it might have germs on it. This waste gets cleaned up in a special way that's different from your garbage at home. Regular garbage, like food wrappers, goes into regular bins. The hospital sorts everything carefully to keep the place safe and clean for everyone.

instruction: Can I bring snacks from home?
response: That depends! Before eating anything, you should always check with your nurse first because some kids are on special diets or need to avoid eating before procedures. If your care team says it's okay, your family can keep some personal snacks in the family fridge — just make sure they're labelled with your name and the date! There are also pantries on the B6 unit with drinks and light snacks for patients.

instruction: Why do some doors have codes on them?
response: Some areas of the hospital have special door codes to keep patients extra safe. For example, the B6 inpatient unit is a locked unit, and when you're admitted, you'll get a secret code to use. It's kind of like a password! It makes sure only people who belong on that floor can get in, which helps keep everyone secure.

instruction: Why can't I have perfume or body spray here?
response: The hospital is a fragrance-free place, which means no perfume, body spray, or strong-smelling products. That's because some patients and staff are really sensitive to smells — strong fragrances can give them headaches, make it hard to breathe, or even cause allergic reactions. So leaving the smelly stuff at home is a kind thing to do for everyone around you!

instruction: What does the Social Worker do?
response: A social worker is someone at the hospital who helps your family with all the non-medical stuff that can be stressful. They can help your parents figure out paperwork, find support in your community, or just talk through how they're feeling. They're a really helpful person to know about, especially when your family needs extra support. Your nurse can connect your family with one!

instruction: What does an occupational therapist do?
response: An occupational therapist — sometimes called an OT — helps you learn or re-learn everyday things like getting dressed, eating, writing, or playing. If your body needs some extra help doing the things you normally do, the OT comes up with fun ways to practise and get better at them. They're really creative and good at making activities that feel more like play than work!

instruction: What's a dietitian?
response: A dietitian is a food expert! At the hospital, the dietitian makes sure you're getting the right kinds of foods to help your body heal and feel strong. If you have allergies or need a special diet, they're the person who helps figure out what's safe and yummy for you to eat. If you have any questions about your food, your nurse can ask the dietitian to come chat with you.

instruction: What is a nurse practitioner?
response: A nurse practitioner is someone who is kind of like a mix between a nurse and a doctor. They've done lots of extra school and training, so they can do many of the same things a doctor does — like figuring out what's wrong and planning your care. They work really closely with your doctor and are another important member of your care team!

instruction: Why does the nurse scan my bracelet before giving me medicine?
response: Your bracelet has a barcode on it — just like the barcodes on items at the grocery store! When the nurse scans it, the computer checks to make sure the right medicine is going to the right patient. It's a super important safety step that happens every single time. Pretty smart system, right?

instruction: What is Upopolis?
response: Upopolis is a free, safe website just for kids aged 8 to 18 who are in hospitals across Canada. It lets you connect with other kids who are going through something similar. You can chat, share stories, and make friends. There are laptops you can borrow through Child Life Services to use it. Ask a Child Life Specialist if you want to check it out!

instruction: What is the numbing cream for?
response: The numbing cream is part of something called the Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital. Before you get a needle, the nurse can put a special cream on your skin that makes it go a bit numb, so the poke hurts a lot less. It works kind of like magic — it tells the nerves in your skin to take a little nap! You can always ask for it before a needle procedure.

instruction: What does a physiotherapist do?
response: A physiotherapist — sometimes called a physio — helps you with moving your body. If you had surgery or an injury, they'll teach you exercises and movements to help your muscles get strong again. They might also help you learn to walk with crutches or figure out the safest way to get in and out of a car. They're like a coach for your body!

instruction: Why do some rooms have two beds?
response: Some hospital rooms are shared between two patients. Each patient gets their own space with a curtain they can pull for privacy. The hospital tries to give you the room you'd like, but it depends on which rooms are available and sometimes on what kind of care you need. Even in a shared room, the nurses make sure you feel comfortable and looked after!

instruction: Why can't I eat before my test?
response: Some tests and procedures need your tummy to be completely empty to work properly and to keep you safe. If there's food in your stomach, it could cause problems during certain procedures. I know being hungry isn't fun at all, but your nurse will let you know the second you're allowed to eat again! It's one of those things that's worth the wait.

instruction: What is the hand sanitizer for?
response: The hand sanitizer dispensers you see everywhere are filled with a special alcohol-based gel that kills germs on your hands in seconds. It's the fastest way to clean your hands in the hospital! You should use it before going into a patient room, when leaving a room, and before eating. Just squirt some on and rub your hands together — easy peasy!

instruction: How is Children's Hospital laid out? It's confusing.
response: Totally understandable — it's a big building. Children's Hospital is in Zone B of the Victoria Hospital site at 800 Commissioners Road East in London. Room numbers tell you exactly where you are: the first letter is the zone, the next number is the floor. So B6-261 means Zone B, floor 6, room 261. There's an app called MazeMap you can download that has a full interactive map, and you can scan QR codes near elevator bays to pull up maps too. Information desks are also staffed Monday–Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.

instruction: What's with the hospital smell?
response: That distinctive smell is mostly industrial-strength disinfectants used to keep every surface as sterile as possible. Hospitals have very strict cleaning protocols because patients with compromised immune systems are particularly vulnerable to infections. You might also be noticing hand sanitizer — the alcohol-based kind is used constantly throughout the building. The fact that it's a fragrance-free facility also means you're not getting the mix of perfumes and products you'd encounter elsewhere, which can make the antiseptic smell more noticeable.

instruction: Why do they need to check my identity so many times?
response: It might feel repetitive, but it's one of the most critical patient safety protocols in any hospital. Every time someone checks your armband — which has your name, date of birth, hospital ID, and a barcode — they're verifying they have the right patient before giving medication, running a test, or starting a procedure. Mix-ups in hospitals can have serious consequences, so this is a hard rule that applies to everyone. If you have allergies, you'll also have a red bracelet so every member of your team is aware.

instruction: Why do I have to wear this wristband?
response: Your armband is your hospital ID — it has your name, date of birth, hospital ID number, and a scannable barcode. Staff check or scan it before every medication, test, or procedure as a safety measure to prevent any mix-ups. If you have allergies, you'll also have a red allergy bracelet. Babies under one year get a security alarm band as well. It's not optional — it's one of the most important safety measures in the hospital.

instruction: Why is the hospital fragrance-free?
response: LHSC has a fragrance-free policy because scented products — cologne, perfume, scented lotions, even hair products — can trigger allergic reactions and respiratory distress in patients and staff. In a hospital where many people have compromised immune systems or sensitive airways, even common fragrances can cause real problems. The policy covers the entire facility, including all buildings, grounds, and parking lots.

instruction: Why aren't latex balloons allowed?
response: Latex allergies can range from mild skin irritation to severe anaphylaxis, which is a life-threatening reaction. Since hospitals treat immunocompromised and allergy-prone patients, even airborne latex particles could put someone at risk. That's why LHSC bans latex balloons completely. If you want to brighten someone's room, mylar (foil) balloons are a safe alternative. Interestingly, poinsettia plants are also banned because they contain a compound similar to what's found in rubber latex.

instruction: What's the purpose of the weapons detection system at the ER?
response: LHSC has introduced a weapons detection system at their Emergency Department entrances as a security measure. Everyone entering the ED walks through it — including children, who are scanned with their parent or guardian present. The technology is non-invasive, meaning you don't have to stop, empty your pockets, or remove anything. If the system flags something, a trained security guard will check. There are accommodations available if you need them — just speak with the security guard at the entrance.

instruction: What's the Wi-Fi situation here?
response: The hospital has free Wi-Fi available. You can connect your phone, laptop, or tablet to it. There's also a patient entertainment site where you can stream live Rogers TV for free or log into your own accounts on services like Netflix. If you run into connection issues, you or your family can call the Data Valet service at 1-800-642-3958 for help.

instruction: What's the difference between a resident and a medical student?
response: Medical students are still in medical school — they've graduated university and are completing their MD degree. Residents have already finished medical school and earned their degree, and they're now doing hands-on specialty training. Both may be involved in your care, but they're always supervised by attending physicians. It's a layered system: the attending physician oversees residents, who in turn oversee medical students. You have every right to ask who's who on your care team.

instruction: What does a nurse practitioner do compared to a regular nurse or doctor?
response: Nurse practitioners (NPs) sit somewhere between registered nurses and physicians in terms of scope. They've completed advanced education — typically a master's degree — and can assess patients, order tests, diagnose conditions, and plan treatment, much like a doctor. At Children's Hospital, NPs work closely with attending physicians and function similarly to residents. Registered nurses focus more on day-to-day patient care: administering medications, monitoring vitals, coordinating appointments, and being the consistent face you see during your stay.

instruction: What is a Child Life Specialist, and would they even work with teens?
response: Child Life Specialists work with patients of all ages, including teens. They're professionals trained to help you cope with the stress of hospitalization. For teens, that might look like preparing you for a scary procedure, teaching pain management or coping techniques, or just being someone outside your medical team you can talk to honestly. They're not therapists and they're not there to babysit you — they're there to help you process what you're going through and advocate for your comfort.

instruction: What does a social worker at the hospital actually do?
response: Hospital social workers provide emotional support and practical help. They can assist your family with things like navigating the hospital system, accessing community services, handling insurance or financial challenges, and communicating with your care team when things get complicated. They can also help with discharge planning, school transitions, and connecting you with mental health resources. If you or your family are feeling overwhelmed by anything beyond your medical care, a social worker is the person to ask about.

instruction: Who are the people at the information desk?
response: They're typically volunteers and staff whose job is to help you navigate the building. Information desks at Children's Hospital are open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. and from noon to 4 p.m. on weekends. You can also find guide volunteers at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. They can help with directions, answer general questions, and point you to the right department.

instruction: What is a spiritual care specialist?
response: Spiritual care at LHSC is a professional service that supports all patients and families regardless of religious beliefs — or lack thereof. Spiritual care practitioners can help with things like grief, existential questions, finding meaning during a difficult time, or simply having someone listen without judgment. The hospital also has a Sanctuary (room C3-402) open 24/7 for quiet reflection, prayer, or meditation. You can request a spiritual care visit through your nurse using pager 14693.

instruction: Why do so many different people come into my room?
response: Hospital care is team-based. Your team might include an attending physician, residents, nurse practitioners, registered nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, dietitians, social workers, and more — each responsible for a different aspect of your health. It can feel like a revolving door, but each person has a specific role. You're absolutely entitled to ask anyone who enters your room to identify themselves and explain why they're there. If the traffic is overwhelming, let your nurse know.

instruction: Can I ask to see a psychologist?
response: Yes. Children's Hospital has paediatric psychology services available. Psychologists can help with things like adjusting to illness, managing anxiety or stress related to your condition, and developing coping strategies for physical, emotional, and behavioural symptoms. They can also assess cognitive and learning impacts if your medical condition affects those. Talk to your nurse or your care team and they can arrange a referral.

instruction: How does a pulse oximeter actually work?
response: A pulse oximeter clips onto your finger and uses two wavelengths of light — one red, one infrared — that pass through your fingertip. Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin absorb these wavelengths differently, so a sensor on the other side of the clip reads the ratio and calculates your blood oxygen saturation (SpO2). It also picks up your pulse rate from the fluctuation in blood volume with each heartbeat. It's completely non-invasive, painless, and gives results in seconds.

instruction: What do all those numbers on the monitor mean?
response: The bedside monitor typically displays several vital signs. Heart rate (HR) is how many times your heart beats per minute. Blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) shows the percentage of oxygen-carrying haemoglobin in your blood. Blood pressure might show as two numbers (systolic/diastolic). Respiratory rate (RR) tracks your breaths per minute. Each parameter has an acceptable range, and the monitor alarms if a reading falls outside that range. If you want to know what your specific numbers mean, ask your nurse — they can walk you through what's normal for you.

instruction: Why does the IV pump keep beeping?
response: IV pumps are designed to be cautious — they'll alarm for a range of reasons. The most common ones are: the bag is nearly empty, there's a kink in the line, a bubble of air has been detected, or the flow is being blocked (sometimes just from bending your arm). It doesn't usually mean something is wrong. Your nurse will silence the alarm and fix whatever triggered it. If a pump is beeping and nobody comes quickly, press your call button.

instruction: How does an MRI work?
response: An MRI — magnetic resonance imaging — uses powerful magnets and radio waves to create detailed images of the inside of your body, without radiation. You lie in a tube-shaped machine that generates a strong magnetic field, which causes hydrogen atoms in your body to align. Radio wave pulses knock them out of alignment, and as they realign, they emit signals that a computer processes into images. It's loud (you'll hear knocking and humming), it takes a while, and you need to stay still, but it's not painful. If you're anxious about it, let your team know — there are ways they can help.

instruction: Why do they need to take my blood so often?
response: Blood tests give your care team a snapshot of what's happening inside your body — things like blood cell counts, electrolyte levels, organ function markers, and inflammation indicators. If your condition is changing or you're on certain medications, they need to monitor these values regularly to adjust your treatment plan. Each draw is usually a small amount, and it's tracked carefully. If the frequency is bothering you, it's worth asking your team to explain exactly why each one is needed.

instruction: What's the Comfort Promise?
response: The Comfort Promise is Children's Hospital's commitment to managing pain and anxiety during needle procedures using evidence-based strategies. These include topical anaesthetic cream to numb the skin, comfort positioning (sitting upright in supportive positions rather than being held down), distraction techniques like watching a video, and for infants, sucrose or breastfeeding. Research shows that untreated needle pain can lead to long-term health care avoidance and increased pain sensitivity in future procedures. You can always ask for these strategies before any needle procedure — it's your right.

instruction: What is a CT scan?
response: A CT (computed tomography) scan is essentially a series of X-ray images taken from different angles, which a computer combines into cross-sectional slices of your body. It gives much more detail than a regular X-ray and can show soft tissue, blood vessels, and bones. The machine looks like a large donut — you lie on a table that slides through the centre. The scan itself is painless and usually quick, though you might need contrast dye injected through an IV to make certain structures more visible.

instruction: What does an ECG measure?
response: An ECG — electrocardiogram — records the electrical activity of your heart. Those sticky pads (electrodes) placed on your chest, arms, and legs detect the tiny electrical signals generated each time your heart beats. The ECG produces a tracing that shows the rhythm, rate, and electrical pattern. Cardiologists can read these tracings to identify irregular rhythms, structural issues, or other heart-related conditions. It's non-invasive, painless, and takes just a few minutes.

instruction: Can I keep using my phone in the hospital?
response: Absolutely. The hospital encourages patients to use their own phones to stay connected with friends and family. There's free Wi-Fi, and the patient telephones are available for free local and toll-free calls too. Just be mindful in shared spaces — keep the volume reasonable, use headphones when you can, and be aware that some areas might ask you to silence your phone for medical reasons.

instruction: What can I actually do for entertainment here?
response: More than you might expect. The hospital has a patient entertainment site with free live TV and the ability to use your own streaming accounts. There's a School-Age Activity Room (B6-065) with games, crafts, puzzles, and LEGO. The SMILE Room (B6-261) is a sensory room with fibre optics, bubble columns, and music. Upopolis is a free, secure social network for patients aged 8–18. There's also music therapy, art therapy, and the Heroes' Circle martial arts program. Ask a Child Life Specialist what's available during your stay.

instruction: Is there anywhere private I can go in this hospital?
response: There are a few options. The Quiet Rooms on B6 (rooms B6-119 and B6-257) are available for private conversations, phone calls, or just needing a moment to yourself — check with your nurse or unit clerk before using them. The Sanctuary (C3-402) is open 24/7 for quiet reflection. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre (B1-006) offers a quieter space as well. If you just need space from the constant activity in your room, let your nurse know and they can help you find somewhere.

instruction: Can I leave my room and walk around?
response: That depends on your care plan. Some patients are free to move around the unit or visit common areas like the activity rooms or the family lounge (Culliton Family Lounge, B6-110). Others may have restrictions depending on their condition, IV lines, or infection control precautions. Always check with your nurse first. If you have an IV, you can usually bring the pole with you — it's on wheels. If you want to visit areas outside your unit, you'll definitely need to clear it with your team.

instruction: What food options are there if I'm vegetarian?
response: The hospital offers vegetarian options as part of its patient food menu, including vegan meals and vegetarian options with dairy and eggs, or dairy, eggs, and fish. They also accommodate halal, kosher, and allergy-specific diets. You'll get a form with your breakfast tray where you can choose your meals for the next day. If you have specific preferences or concerns, ask your nurse to connect you with a dietitian — they can help customize your meals.

instruction: What time are meals served?
response: Breakfast is delivered between 7:45 and 8:45 a.m., lunch between 11:45 a.m. and 12:45 p.m., and dinner between 4:45 and 5:45 p.m. If you want something between meals, the B6 inpatient unit has pantries (B6-149 and B6-231) stocked with drinks and light snacks. There are also vending machines near the elevators in Zone B on the 1st and 3rd floors. Always check with your care team before eating, especially before tests or procedures.

instruction: Can I store my own food here?
response: Yes — there's a family fridge with a freezer available for personal food storage. Just label everything with your name and the date. The hospital can't be responsible for food that gets removed from the fridge by mistake. If you're on the B6 inpatient unit, the pantries are in rooms B6-149 and B6-231. The PCCU also has a small fridge in the waiting room. Always check with your care team about any dietary restrictions before eating food from home.

instruction: Where's the closest coffee or food I can buy?
response: 'On the Go featuring Tim Hortons' is right on the second floor of Zone B in the main atrium. It's open weekdays from 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. but closed on weekends and holidays. Vending machines with snacks and drinks are near the elevators on the 1st and 3rd floors of Zone B, and there are ATMs there too. A full list of on-site food options is on the LHSC website.

instruction: Who has access to my medical information?
response: Your personal health information (PHI) can only be shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). At LHSC, you have the right to consent to or refuse the collection, use, and disclosure of your health information, to access your records, to request corrections, to know who's seen your records, and to be notified if your information is accessed inappropriately. If you have concerns about your privacy, the hospital's privacy office can be reached at 519-685-8500 extension 32996 or privacy@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: Can I have a say in my own care?
response: Absolutely. Children's Hospital sees families — and that includes you — as partners in care. You're encouraged to ask questions, request explanations of any tests or treatments, understand the risks and benefits, and express your preferences. There's even a formal process called Shared Decision Making where patients work with care teams and a Decision Coach to make informed choices. You're also invited to participate in bedside shift change reports where nurses review your care plan. Don't hesitate to speak up — your voice matters.

instruction: Can I ask the doctors to explain what's happening to me?
response: Yes, and you should. You have every right to understand your care plan, your diagnosis, what tests are being ordered and why, what medications you're taking, and what the expected outcomes are. If something isn't clear, ask them to explain it differently. If you feel like you're being talked around rather than talked to, let your care team know — you can also ask your nurse to help facilitate better communication.

instruction: What if I have a complaint about my care?
response: Start by talking directly to your care team — they may be able to resolve it quickly. If that doesn't work, LHSC has a Patient Relations office you can contact. They're reachable by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca, by phone at 519-685-8500 extension 52036, or via a contact form on the LHSC website. They handle questions, concerns, and formal feedback about care experiences. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

instruction: What if I need an interpreter?
response: LHSC offers free interpretation services for patients who are most comfortable speaking in a language other than English, or for those who are deaf, deafened, or hard of hearing. Just ask your care team to arrange one. They can also set up sign language or deaf-blind translation. You're entitled to communicate with your care team in a language you're comfortable with — never hesitate to ask for this.

instruction: Why do hospitals use so much hand sanitizer instead of just soap?
response: Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) is actually the preferred hand hygiene method in hospitals when hands aren't visibly dirty. It's faster, more effective against most pathogens, and can be placed at point-of-care — meaning right outside every room and at every bedside. The alcohol denatures the proteins of bacteria and viruses almost instantly. Soap and water is reserved for visibly soiled hands or specific situations like C. difficile, since alcohol doesn't kill those spores. It's all about efficiency and accessibility in a setting where hand hygiene compliance literally saves lives.

instruction: Why do I have to fast before surgery?
response: When you're under general anaesthesia, the reflexes that normally prevent stomach contents from entering your lungs are suppressed. If there's food or liquid in your stomach, it could come back up and be aspirated into your lungs, which can cause a serious condition called aspiration pneumonia. Fasting guidelines are based on evidence about how long different types of food and liquid take to leave the stomach. It's not fun, but it's one of the most important pre-surgical safety measures.

instruction: What's the point of a blood pressure reading?
response: Blood pressure measures the force your blood exerts against your arterial walls. The two numbers you see — systolic (the higher one) and diastolic (the lower one) — represent the pressure when your heart contracts and when it relaxes between beats, respectively. Monitoring it helps your team detect things like dehydration, blood loss, infection response, or cardiac issues. In a hospital setting, it's checked frequently because changes can be an early warning sign that something needs attention.

instruction: Why are hospitals so concerned about infection control?
response: Hospitals bring together a concentration of vulnerable patients — people with weakened immune systems, open wounds, surgical sites, and invasive devices like IVs. Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are a real and significant risk. The infection prevention protocols you see — hand hygiene, isolation precautions, gowns, gloves, restricted visitor policies during outbreaks — all exist because the evidence shows they meaningfully reduce transmission. It's one of those areas where small, consistent actions have outsized impact.

instruction: What's the difference between an X-ray, CT scan, MRI, and ultrasound?
response: They all image the inside of your body but use different technology. X-rays use ionizing radiation and are best for bones and detecting fluid in lungs — quick and simple. CT scans also use X-rays but take cross-sectional slices, giving much more detail for soft tissue, organs, and blood vessels. MRIs use magnetic fields and radio waves — no radiation — and excel at soft tissue detail like the brain, spinal cord, and joints. Ultrasound uses sound waves and is great for real-time imaging, like watching blood flow or examining organs. Each has trade-offs in terms of detail, time, cost, and radiation exposure.

instruction: What do white blood cells actually do?
response: White blood cells (WBCs) are a key part of your immune system. There are several types, each with a different job. Neutrophils are first responders that engulf and destroy bacteria. Lymphocytes include T-cells (which coordinate the immune response and kill infected cells) and B-cells (which produce antibodies). Monocytes clean up dead cells and debris. Eosinophils fight parasites and are involved in allergic responses. When your doctors check your blood count, WBC levels help them understand how your immune system is functioning. If you have questions about your specific results, your care team can explain what they mean for you.

instruction: Why do some medications come through an IV instead of as a pill?
response: Several reasons. Some medications are broken down by stomach acid and would lose their effectiveness if swallowed. IV delivery also gets medication into your bloodstream immediately, which matters when timing is critical. Dosing can be more precisely controlled through an IV infusion. Some patients can't take anything by mouth — they might be nil by mouth before a procedure, nauseous, or unconscious. And certain medications are too irritating to the GI tract. Your care team chooses the delivery method based on what's most effective and safe for your specific situation.

instruction: Can my friends visit me?
response: Yes. The general visitor policy allows up to two care partners at the bedside at one time for inpatients. Visiting is flexible and varies by unit and patient condition, so check with your unit's staff about optimal times. Visitors need to practice hand hygiene before and after visiting, and shouldn't come if they've been sick in the last week. Overnight visitors (between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m.) are asked to stay in the patient's room and notify unit staff when arriving and leaving.

instruction: I'm bored out of my mind. What is there to do?
response: I get it — hospital stays can drag. Here's what's available: the School-Age Activity Room (B6-065) has board games, puzzles, crafts, and LEGO. The SMILE Room (B6-261) is a sensory room with bubble columns and fibre optics. There's art therapy, music therapy, and the Heroes' Circle martial arts program. Upopolis is a secure social network for patients aged 8–18. You've got free TV and can use your own streaming services over Wi-Fi. The Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110) is a space to hang out with visitors. And ask Child Life about any special events — they run activities regularly.

instruction: What is Upopolis?
response: Upopolis is a free, secure social networking platform specifically for paediatric patients aged 8–18 across Canadian hospitals. It lets you connect with other patients who get what you're going through. You can chat, share stories, and find community. Laptops are available through Child Life Services if you need one. If you're interested, ask a Child Life Specialist to help you get set up.

instruction: Can I have some control over when people come into my room?
response: To some extent, yes. Certain visits — vital sign checks, medication administration, physician rounds — are scheduled and necessary. But for non-urgent things, you can talk to your nurse about coordinating visits to give you blocks of uninterrupted time, especially for sleeping, studying, or just having privacy. The quiet rooms on B6 (B6-119 and B6-257) are also available for private time. You're a partner in your care, and reasonable requests about your schedule and space are respected.

instruction: What support is there for trans or gender-diverse patients?
response: Children's Hospital has a dedicated Gender Pathways Service (GPS) that provides gender-affirming care for children and teens 17 and under. It's a multidisciplinary service that follows guidelines from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health and other North American and international standards. If you'd like to learn more or access the service, you can contact them directly at gps@lhsc.on.ca or ask your care team for a referral.

instruction: Is there support for Indigenous patients?
response: Yes. The Youth Indigenous Wellness Program has a consultant who supports mental health and cultural wellness for Indigenous children accessing care at Children's Hospital. They bridge traditional ways of knowing with western approaches to healing. There's also an Indigenous Healing Space (E1-204) that's available with priority given to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous patients and families. You can ask your care team or contact the hospital's Indigenous Health team by email at IndigenousHealth@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: Are there resources for Black patients and families navigating care?
response: LHSC has a Black Health Navigator program. Black Health Navigators are trained and registered healthcare workers who help Black patients and families navigate the health system — they provide information on healthcare options and help ensure your voice is heard during conversations with your care team. You can access this through your care team or by emailing BlackHealth@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: What if I'm asked to participate in a research study?
response: Research participation is always voluntary. During your stay, a physician or research team member might ask if you'd like to join a study. All studies conducted at LHSC are reviewed and approved by the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute and a Research Ethics Board. You'll receive a detailed Letter of Information about the study. Take your time, ask as many questions as you need, and review it thoroughly. Saying no will not affect your care in any way. If you have concerns, you can contact the Quality Assurance and Education Team at researchqualityandeducation@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: What's the bedside shift change report?
response: It's a handoff process that happens when one nursing shift ends and another begins. The outgoing and incoming nurses review your care plan together, and you and your family are invited to listen and participate. The incoming nurse introduces themselves, they go over your care plan, complete safety checks, and ask if you have questions or anything to add. It typically takes three to five minutes. It's a good opportunity to stay informed about your care and flag anything the team might not know.

instruction: How does the hospital handle allergies?
response: If you have allergies, you'll be given a red allergy bracelet so every member of your care team can see it immediately. Your allergies will also be documented in your medical record. The food services team can accommodate allergy-specific diets — including priority allergens like eggs, milk, mustard, nuts, and more. The nursing staff and pharmacists check for drug allergies before administering any medication. If you develop a new allergy or sensitivity during your stay, tell your nurse right away.

instruction: Why do nurses change every 12 hours?
response: Nursing shifts at Children's Hospital run roughly 12 hours, with handovers at around 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (shift changes happen between 6:45 and 7:30 a.m./p.m.). This structure ensures nurses are alert and performing at their best — patient safety research shows that fatigue increases the risk of errors. The trade-off is continuity, which is why the bedside shift report is so important. It ensures all your information transfers accurately between nurses.

instruction: Why are visiting hours not the same on every unit?
response: Different units have different patient needs and care intensities. For example, the NICU and PCCU have stricter access because those patients are more vulnerable. Visiting policies are based on the condition and care needs of each patient, privacy considerations for other patients, and infection control requirements — especially during outbreaks, when only essential care partners are permitted. The flexibility is intentional so each unit can prioritize what's best for the patients on it.

instruction: What happens when I'm discharged?
response: Your care team will go over everything with you and your family: medications (purpose, dosage, timing, side effects), any dietary changes, activity restrictions, follow-up appointments, and what to watch for at home. You'll receive written instructions. If you need equipment or home care services, those need to be assessed by an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator before you leave. If your stay was longer than 14 days, a new referral to Ontario Health atHome is needed. Make sure you understand everything before you leave — and don't be afraid to ask questions.

instruction: Do I need a car seat when I leave?
response: By law, children must travel in an approved car seat. Your family should bring your car seat when they come to pick you up. If your condition has changed or you have new mobility needs, a physiotherapist or occupational therapist will help figure out safe transportation options. LHSC's Trauma Program also offers consultations with certified Car Seat Technicians to make sure the seat is properly installed.

instruction: Will the hospital help me transition back to school?
response: Yes. The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital specifically supports key transition milestones, including moving from hospital back to school. They can help you and your family communicate with your school about any accommodations or modifications you might need. Your social worker can also help coordinate this. It's a good idea to talk with your care team about school re-entry early so everything is in place before discharge.

instruction: What's the Paediatric Family Resource Centre?
response: It's located on the 1st floor of Zone B (room B1-006) and it offers patients and family members peer support, help with forms and applications, and access to information on children's health topics from a lived-experience lens. Hours are Monday, Wednesday, Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; Tuesday and Thursday from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m.; and Saturday and Sunday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. by appointment. It's also a quieter space to step away from the unit for a bit.

instruction: Why is there security at the hospital?
response: Security exists to keep everyone — patients, families, and staff — safe. They patrol the building, manage after-hours access (the B Tower entrance locks at 8:30 p.m. and is controlled by security after that), respond to emergencies, and can escort you to your car or to the Ronald McDonald House if needed. You can reach security dispatch at extension 52281. The emergency response extension is 55555. They're a resource, not something to be worried about.

instruction: Can I go outside the hospital during my stay?
response: That's up to your care team and depends on your condition. Some patients may be able to visit outdoor spaces like Alex's Butterfly Garden (D Zone, Level 2), which is a peaceful landscaped area with benches and a water fountain. Others may have restrictions due to their care plan, IV lines, or infection control precautions. Always get permission from your nurse first. If you're feeling cooped up, let your team know — sometimes even a brief change of scenery helps.

instruction: What's Alex's Butterfly Garden?
response: It's an outdoor garden in D Zone, Level 2, created by the Hart Family in partnership with the Children's Health Foundation. It was built in honour of perinatal and infant loss and offers a tranquil environment with benches and a water fountain. It's open to children, families, and staff as a space for quiet reflection and fresh air. You can find it on MazeMap or ask for directions.

instruction: Why do some rooms require you to wear a gown, gloves, and mask before entering?
response: Those are additional infection control precautions, also called isolation precautions. They're in place when a patient has an infection that could spread to others or when a patient's immune system is so compromised that they need extra protection from outside germs. The specific gear depends on the type of precaution — contact precautions typically require gloves and a gown, droplet precautions add a mask, and airborne precautions may require an N95 respirator. Always check with staff before entering a room with a precaution sign.

instruction: How does the hospital accommodate different dietary and religious needs?
response: LHSC offers a variety of therapeutic, allergy-based, and religious-based diets. That includes vegan, vegetarian (with various inclusions), halal, kosher, and pork-free options, as well as accommodation for priority allergens like eggs, milk, mustard, and nuts. You'll choose from a menu each day based on your prescribed diet. If your dietary needs aren't being met, talk to your nurse and they can involve a dietitian.

instruction: Why do I keep getting woken up at night?
response: Night checks are part of standard nursing care. Your nurse needs to periodically assess your vital signs, check your IV, and make sure you're safe and comfortable. The frequency depends on your condition — some patients are checked every few hours, others more frequently. They try to be as unobtrusive as possible. If the disruptions are seriously affecting your sleep, talk to your care team about whether the frequency can be adjusted or if any checks can be consolidated.

instruction: What are Bravery Beads?
response: Bravery Beads is a voluntary program where each bead represents a different element of your care or treatment — an IV insertion, a blood draw, a surgery, an MRI, etc. Over time, you build a personal record of what you've been through. It's available for patients of all ages dealing with long-term or chronic conditions. Some people find it a meaningful way to track and acknowledge their experience. Ask your care team or a Child Life Specialist if you'd like to participate.

instruction: What is the pharmacy at Children's Hospital?
response: The Children's Hospital Pharmacy and Compounding Centre is on the first floor (B1-001), right near the B1 entrance. It's open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. excluding holidays. You can fill prescriptions there before you leave, which is convenient for discharge day. They also sell breast pump kits. If you have questions about any of your medications, your nurse can arrange for a pharmacist to come talk to you directly. The pharmacy's extension is 58082.

instruction: What if I need legal help related to my hospital stay?
response: There's actually a program for that. Pro Bono Law Ontario (PBLO) has a partnership with Children's Hospital that helps families identify and resolve legal issues that could impact a child's health or the family's ability to provide care. It provides free legal assistance to low-income families whose child is an inpatient or outpatient. Your social worker can refer your case to the on-site triage lawyer.

instruction: Can I get therapy dog visits?
response: Children's Hospital has partnered with St. John Ambulance to offer a therapy dog program on several units. These are certified therapy dogs that are trained to be calm and gentle. Research supports that interacting with therapy dogs can improve a patient's sense of wellbeing and support rehabilitation. Ask your care team if there's a scheduled visit on your unit. Regular pet visits from home aren't typically allowed, but compassionate exceptions can be considered with manager approval, proof of vaccination, and a signed waiver.

instruction: What's the deal with the smoke-free policy?
response: LHSC is completely smoke-free in compliance with the Smoke-Free Ontario Act. That means all buildings, all grounds, and all parking lots — including smoking inside cars on hospital property. The policy covers cigarettes, e-cigarettes, vapes, cigars, pipes, and any other substance that can be smoked, including marijuana. The one exception is the traditional use of tobacco by Indigenous peoples for cultural or spiritual purposes — there's a designated space for that.

instruction: How does the hospital handle pain management for teens?
response: Children's Hospital follows the Comfort Promise, which is their commitment to evidence-based pain and anxiety management. For needle procedures, that includes topical anaesthetics, comfort positioning (upright and supportive, not restraining), and distraction techniques. Beyond needles, your care team assesses and manages pain as part of your overall care plan. You should always communicate openly about your pain levels — there's no benefit to toughing it out, and untreated pain can actually slow recovery. Ask your team about what options are available for your specific situation.

instruction: What does 'Zone' mean in the hospital's layout?
response: The Victoria Hospital site is divided into lettered zones — A, B, C, D, E — each representing a different section of the building. Children's Hospital is in Zone B. Room numbers encode location: the first letter is the zone, the next digit is the floor, and the remaining numbers are the room. So B6-261 = Zone B, floor 6, room 261. Understanding the zone system makes navigating the building a lot easier. There's also an app called MazeMap and on-site QR codes that pull up interactive maps.

instruction: What if my family lives far from London?
response: If your family lives outside London, the Ronald McDonald House is a nearby accommodation option specifically for families with a child in the hospital. Your care team can help determine eligibility and connect your family. There's also a Ronald McDonald Family Room right in the hospital (extension 56896). LHSC maintains a list of local hotels and motels on their website, and some offer discounted 'hospital rates' upon request. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre can also help your family navigate logistics.
